specAnchors.text: be able to calculate the entropy change of the system for a reaction, ∆ S system , given the entropies of the reactants and products
be able to calculate the entropy change in the surroundings, and hence ∆ S total , using the expression ∆ S surroundings = − ∆ H T

primer.text: A spontaneous change must be judged on the system and the surroundings together. The system contribution comes from standard entropies of products minus reactants; the surroundings contribution equals the enthalpy change transferred divided by temperature, with a minus sign. This note computes both pieces and their sum, in J K-1 mol-1, from data-book values.

modules.title: System plus surroundings
modules.opening: Sodium burns in chlorine despite forming an ordered solid from a solid and a gas - the system's entropy falls. The puzzle resolves by counting the surroundings too: the huge released heat scatters energy through them, and their entropy gain swamps the system's loss.
keyPoints: The reaction 2Na plus Cl2 forming 2NaCl is very exothermic yet decreases the system's entropy, as a solid forms from a solid and a gas.
The resolution counts the surroundings: released energy creates a large entropy rise there, with more ways of arranging quanta outside the system.
The total entropy change is delta S total = delta S system + delta S surroundings.
For sodium and chlorine, the strongly positive delta S surroundings outweighs the negative delta S system, so the change is spontaneous.

low.restatement: Add both books: delta S total = delta S system + delta S surroundings; the surroundings' gain, driven by released heat, can pay for the system's loss.
low.analogy: Tidying one messy drawer by dumping its contents in a big spare cupboard: the drawer (system) looks neat, the cupboard (surroundings) absorbs the chaos and still has room to spare.
low.examPointer: Always compute both terms before judging feasibility - a negative system term is not a verdict.

medium.restatement: Energy released by the system does not vanish; it lands in the surroundings and spreads there, which is why an exothermic change can buy back any local order it creates.
medium.analogy: A radiator warms the whole room while cooling itself relative to the room: heat moves and spreads.
medium.examPointer: The spontaneity verdict belongs to delta S total, never to delta S system alone.

modules.title: Entropy change of the system
modules.opening: The system's contribution comes straight from data books: sum the standard entropies of the products, subtract the reactants', and mind the stoichiometry. Elements are not awarded zero entropy - unlike enthalpies of formation - and the unit is joules, not kilojoules.
keyPoints: Entropy changes run an order of magnitude below enthalpy changes, which is why entropy carries the smaller unit J K^-1 mol^-1.
The standard entropy change of the system is delta S system = sum of S(products) minus sum of S(reactants).
For N2 plus 3H2 forming 2NH3, the equation is 2 x S(NH3) minus (S(N2) plus 3 x S(H2)).
Unlike enthalpy of formation, standard entropy for elements is not zero; data-book values exist for elements and compounds.

low.restatement: Delta S system = S(products) summed with coefficients minus S(reactants) likewise; elements carry nonzero standard entropies.
low.analogy: A stock-take: count everything leaving the store, subtract everything entering, and respect how many of each moved.
low.examPointer: Watch the stoichiometry - forgetting the coefficient 3 on H2 is the classic slip.

medium.restatement: Standard entropies count what is on the shelf, not what was made there; every species arrives with its own countable disorder, elements included.
medium.analogy: A moving-out inventory: even the landlord's original fittings (elements) have a count, unlike 'formation' which resets to zero.
medium.examPointer: Quote units J K^-1 mol^-1 - the joule scale surprises students after kilojoule enthalpies.

modules.title: Entropy change of the surroundings
modules.opening: The surroundings' gain or loss depends on one transfer: the enthalpy change landing in them. Divide the transferred energy by the temperature and flip the sign - exothermic reactions heat and disorder the surroundings, endothermic ones borrow order from them. The same heat buys more disorder in cold surroundings than in hot ones.
keyPoints: The surroundings' entropy change needs the energy transferred to them, which is the enthalpy change: delta S surroundings = -delta H / T.
T is the absolute temperature in kelvin.
The same quantity of energy produces a greater entropy change in cold surroundings than in hot ones.
Delta H must be converted from kJ mol^-1 to J mol^-1 before the division, since entropy is quoted in J K^-1 mol^-1.
For Al2O3 with carbon at 298 K, delta H = +1336 kJ mol^-1 gives delta S surroundings = -1336000/298 = -4483 J K^-1 mol^-1.

low.restatement: Delta S surroundings = -delta H / T with T in kelvin and delta H in joules; exothermic gives positive, endothermic negative.
low.analogy: A donation to a small village (cold surroundings) changes it more than the same donation to a huge city (hot surroundings).
low.examPointer: Convert kilojoules to joules first - the missing x1000 is the classic mark-loser.

medium.restatement: Temperature is the exchange rate between energy and entropy: heat delivered where quanta are scarce (low T) rearranges more, so the same delta H buys more delta S in colder settings.
medium.analogy: Giving ten sweets to a child with none changes their world; giving the same ten to a sweet-shop owner barely registers.
medium.examPointer: The minus sign encodes direction: heat out (exothermic) enriches the surroundings.

glossary.definition: The sum of the system's and surroundings' entropy changes, the feasibility test.
The data-book entropy S of a substance, nonzero for elements too.
Everything outside the chemical system, which receives or surrenders the enthalpy change.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the total entropy change when 1 mole of sodium chloride forms from its elements in their standard states, given delta S system = -90.1 J K^-1 mol^-1 and delta S surroundings = +1379 J K^-1 mol^-1.
steps: Apply the total entropy equation: delta S total = delta S system + delta S surroundings.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Delta S total = +1289 J K^-1 mol^-1, strongly positive, so the formation is feasible.
